newsitem.title: USA: US SEC starts review of options on Dow averages.
newsitem.headline: US SEC starts review of options on Dow averages.

text.p: The U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission on Tuesday said it has begun its review into the Chicago Board Options Exchange's request to trade options in the Dow Jones Industrial Average and two other related averages.
The agency has started its formal review of the June request by formally seeking the public's view through July 29 on the exchange's proposals.
The Chicago Board Options Exchange has requested approval to list options in the Dow Jones Industrial Average, the Dow Jones Transportation Average and the Dow Jones Utility Average.

The exchange's requests follow the June licensing agreement Dow Jones & Co reached with the Chicago Board of Trade, the American Stock Exchange and the Chicago Board Options Exchange to list futures, options and other products based on the 101-year-old industrial average.
The American Stock Exchange was given permission by the company to trade a unit trust based on the industrial average.
The Chicago Board Options Exchange is asking for the SEC's approval to list and trade cash-settled, European-style stock index options on the Dow Jones Industrial Average.
The widely used Dow Jones Industrial average is a price-weighted index of 30 of the largest, most liquid stocks traded on organized U.S. securities markets.

The utility average is a price-weighted index of 15 of the largest, most liquid U.S. utility stocks and the transportation index is a price-weighted index of 20 of the largest transportation industry stocks.

Options in the DJIA would initially be based on one hundredth of the average but options on an underlying level of one tenth may be introduced later, according to the SEC's notice filed Tuesday in the Federal Register.
"The purpose of offering options based on either one hundredth or one tenth is to offer contracts which appeal to both retail and institutional investors," the SEC said in its notice.

The Chicago Board Options exchange also wants to set minimum increments for bids and offers on the DJIA options at sixteenths of a dollar. Under current rules, bids and offers must be expressed in eighths, excepts for contracts trading below $3.

The exchange proposed setting position limits on the DJIA options at one million contracts for option contracts that are based on one hundredth of the value of the index and 100,000 contracts for those based on one tenth of the value of the index.
